findings.headline: Water safety compliance was materially misstated until a governance review revealed deficiencies in the end-to-end process.
findings.detail: Harlow reported water safety compliance at 100% until a council-initiated deep dive raised concerns about the data. The actual position as of 31 March 2026 was 46.5%, rising to 60% by May 2026 with full compliance projected for September 2026. The council has remediation actions peaking at 13,250 in April 2025, down to fewer than 4,000 by March 2026.
findings.matters: A material misstatement of compliance data suggests control failures in asset management reporting and exposes data integrity risk. The scale of remediation backlog (4,000+ actions outstanding) indicates ongoing operational risk in housing safety. Lenders need confidence in the council's ability to measure and report its true position.

findings.matters: A lender assesses governance stability. The Section 151 Officer is the key position guaranteeing proper financial management and control. findings.paper_title: Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Non-Housing Capital Programme slippage of £13.256 million reprofiled to future years
findings.detail: The Non-Housing Capital Programme delivered £35.069m against an approved £45.602m budget, with £13.256m of expenditure reprofiled into future years. The document states this reflects 'revised delivery programmes,' indicating projects are slower to complete than originally scheduled. This compounds debt service for longer and raises delivery risk.
findings.matters: A lender funding a capital programme needs confidence in delivery timelines. Sustained slippage suggests either project complexity is underestimated or delivery capacity is constrained. Both affect the council's ability to realise benefits and manage debt costs over time.
findings.figures: £35.069m actual vs £45.602m approved; £13.256m reprofiled; capital slippage also material in Housing Programme

findings.matters: A lender wants to understand cost structures and whether they are structural (permanent) or one-off. Growing demand for vulnerable household support suggests increasing social need that may continue and consume operational reserves.

findings.matters: A lender assesses the true cost of maintaining council housing and whether the capital reserve provisions are adequate. Unbudgeted repairs indicate the asset base is more expensive to maintain or in poorer condition than forecast, affecting long-term debt sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: HRA funding capital investment from reserves rather than operations: £4.94 million planned drawdown
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account recorded a planned use of balances of £4.94 million to fund increased capital investment and repairs acceleration approved in July 2025. While HRA balances remain adequate at £9.976 million, this represents the HRA operating at deficit, relying on reserves to fund activity rather than generating surplus.
findings.matters: A lender examining housing revenue sustainability needs to understand whether the HRA generates sufficient operational surplus to fund its capital ambitions. Reserve drawdown is sustainable short-term but if structural, it depletes the buffer against future pressures.
findings.figures: £4.940 million planned drawdown; £9.976 million working balances at 31 March 2026; £2 million minimum recommended balance
findings.quote: Overall, the Housing Revenue Account recorded a planned use of balances of £4.940 million. This reflects the council's strategic decision to support significant investment in council housing while maintaining the long-term sustainability of the 30-year HRA Business Plan.

findings.paper_title: Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: General Fund operating at breakeven: £39,000 surplus on £14.1 million budget
findings.detail: The council achieved only a £39,000 surplus (0.3% of budget) after significant revenue variances. Net service expenditure exceeded revised budget by £2.708 million, offset only by higher-than-expected income from business rates, Council Tax and grants. This leaves essentially no operating headroom.
findings.matters: A lender assesses financial headroom and resilience. Operating at breakeven with no margin means any revenue shortfall or unexpected cost cannot be absorbed from operations and must be met from reserves.
findings.figures: £39,000 surplus; £14.113 million budget; Net Service Expenditure £16.836m vs revised budget £14.129m
findings.quote: The council concluded the financial year with a General Fund surplus of £39,000. While expenditure exceeded the original budget in several areas, this reflected both increased operational activity and investment in priority services.

findings.matters: Capped rent increases limit revenue growth while costs rise. This structural imbalance requires operational efficiencies or subsidy to maintain service levels, reducing the council's ability to improve its financial position through revenue growth.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Capital and Treasury Management 2026-27
findings.headline: The council is borrowing at 4.37% in an economic environment where interest rates remain uncertain and currently at 3.75%.
findings.detail: The treasury strategy assumes new long-term borrowing at 4.37%, up from historical rates. Current Bank Rate is 3.75%. The council is locking in rates at the higher end of the current forecast range, and there is acknowledged uncertainty about whether rates will continue to fall or rise. This creates risk that the council overpays for borrowing if rates continue to decline.
findings.matters: Interest rate risk is material to the affordability of the capital programme. The council's own advisors note that 'long-term borrowing rates are also high' and discuss the incentive to borrow short-term now and refinance later. The decision to borrow long at 4.37% locks in costs but constrains flexibility.
findings.figures: Assumed new long-term borrowing rate: 4.37%; Bank Rate: 3.75%; existing long-term borrowing average rate: 3.51%
findings.quote: gilt yields at the medium and longer end of the curve remain high, and as a result borrowing rates for long term loans are also high ... For the purpose of setting the budget, it has been assumed that new treasury investments will be made at an average rate/yield of 3.09%, and that new long-term loans will be borrowed at an average rate of 4.37%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Capital and Treasury Management 2026-27
findings.headline: The council is not using capital receipts to reduce debt, instead using them for new acquisition spending.
findings.detail: Rather than applying capital receipts to reduce the Capital Financing Requirement (and therefore reduce long-term debt burden), the council has explicitly stated it will use receipts for new spending. This is a choice to increase leverage rather than maintain it, particularly notable when borrowing costs are rising and financing costs are ballooning.
findings.matters: This is a strategic decision to avoid debt reduction. Combined with rising financing costs, it signals the council is prioritising capital expansion over balance sheet consolidation. In a credit review, this would raise questions about the council's medium-term financial resilience if investment returns disappoint.
findings.figures: Capital receipts: £12.399m forecast for 2026/27; none allocated to CFR reduction
findings.quote: Capital receipts can be used to pay off debt and therefore reduce the CFR. The council is proposing to use its capital receipts to reduce future borrowing rather than paying back past borrowing and as such have no plans to utilise capital receipts to reduce the CFR.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Capital and Treasury Management 2026-27
findings.headline: 70% of budgeted 2026/27 capital spend has been reprofiled from 2025/26, indicating slippage in capital delivery.
findings.detail: The NHCP shows £70.489m of expected reprofiling from 2025/26 into 2026/27, representing 75% of the budgeted £92.699m spend for 2026/27. The HCP shows £22.675m of expected slippage from 2025/26. This pattern suggests capital projects are running behind schedule, which risks pushed-forward costs and potential delivery challenges.
findings.matters: Capital project slippage is a red flag for delivery risk. If projects continue to slip, the council will be carrying higher debt for longer without the anticipated asset benefits. This also suggests either overly optimistic budgeting or project management challenges.
findings.figures: 2025/26 NHCP expected slippage £70.489m (75% of 2026/27 budget); HCP slippage £22.675m

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Capital and Treasury Management 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital programme is growing to £203m driven by a borrowing strategy that will more than double net debt by 2029.
findings.detail: The council's capital programme (NHCP £92.7m + HCP £111.3m for 2026/27) represents a substantial increase from prior years, now funded 69% by prudential borrowing. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is forecast to grow from £406.6m (2024/25) to £695.955m (2028/29), an increase of £289.4m. Borrowing is expected to rise from £261.8m to £578.1m to £659.6m over the same period.
findings.matters: The council is undertaking a major expansion of its balance sheet through borrowed capital. Lenders need to understand whether the returns or savings from these investments justify the debt service burden, and whether the council has capacity to absorb an economic downturn without cutting capital or raising other revenue.
findings.figures: CFR rising from £406.6m to £695.955m; forecast borrowing rising from £402.5m (2026) to £659.6m (2029); new borrowing of £289.6m expected in 2026/27 alone

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs are doubling in one year and eating up a third of available revenue.
findings.detail: Interest and MRP costs on the General Fund are forecast to rise from £2.773m to £5.895m in 2026/27, an increase of 113%. As a proportion of net revenue stream, financing costs jump from 17.74% to 35.05%. This represents a sharp affordability deterioration driven by the expanded capital programme and higher borrowing rates.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can absorb this cost of capital from its base revenue. A 35% ratio leaves limited headroom for service pressures or income shocks, and signals that capital-financed activity is consuming a large share of flexible funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - MTFP and General Fund 2026-27 v2
findings.headline: Council is continuing a fifth year of Council Tax freeze while costs rise, creating cumulative funding risk.
findings.detail: Harlow has frozen its share of Council Tax at £288.90 for five consecutive years (since 2021/22). The CFO explicitly flags this risk: 'Although this local decision is currently sustainable, the loss of the cumulative impact does present a financial risk for future unrealised income.' By freezing while costs inflate, the council is losing the ability to grow revenue in line with spending needs.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a predictable revenue source. Continuously freezing it while costs rise (pay, utilities, materials all up substantially) creates a structural erosion of the council's revenue base. Over time, this compounds and forces reliance on reserves, borrowing, or service cuts.

findings.quote: The current MTFP assumes that Harlow's element of the Council Tax level will remain frozen at £288.90 for 2026/27 and future years it has been at this level since 2021/22. This will be kept under review as future budgets are developed. Although this local decision is currently sustainable, the loss of the cumulative impact does present a financial risk for future unrealised income.

findings.matters: The HRA is typically self-financing through rents and the council must manage it separately. A sustained annual deficit eating into HRA reserves is not sustainable. If the HRA balance falls below the £3.5m minimum, the council would face having to cut housing investment or increase rents beyond inflation to restore balance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - MTFP and General Fund 2026-27 v2
findings.headline: Pay inflation budget assumes 3.5% but unions are claiming 10%+ (or £3,000 minimum per employee), creating significant uncontrolled pressure.
findings.detail: The council's pay inflation assumption of 3.5% pa for 2026/27 onwards may be insufficient. The NJC trade union claim of 'at least £3,000 or 10% (whichever is greater)' on all spinal column points substantially exceeds the budgeted amount. If the settlement lands nearer to the union claim, the council would face an immediate budget pressure requiring either savings elsewhere or reserve drawdowns on top of those already planned.
findings.matters: Pay is typically the largest cost base for councils. A 6-7 percentage point variance from budget (if unions get closer to 10% vs 3.5%) across all staff would create material unexpected costs that the council cannot easily control, requiring either service cuts or deeper reserve depletion.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - MTFP and General Fund 2026-27 v2
findings.headline: Business rates collection fund in deficit due to town centre decline and empty properties, with baseline funding assumptions at risk.
findings.detail: The council has a £2.2m collection fund deficit on business rates at 31 March 2026, of which £1.9m relates to 2024/25 and £0.381m to 2025/26. The council explicitly attributes this to 'a historic decline in the town centre and an increase in empty properties.' The CFO notes: 'There is a great deal of volatility in the Business Rates system... The risk arises where the council may fall below the safety net level.' While a collection fund reserve mitigates this, the underlying economic weakness is material.
findings.matters: Town centre decline and rising empty properties indicate local economic weakness that could persist. Business rates are a material funding source (£4.3m baseline funding), and if the town's regeneration does not succeed, this funding could fall below safety-net levels, requiring reserves to compensate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - MTFP and General Fund 2026-27 v2
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation from April 2028 creates material uncertainty, with £0.5m provision acknowledged as potentially insufficient.
findings.detail: The council states clearly that 'From 1 April 2028, Harlow District Council will cease to exist in its current form.' The CFO acknowledges that £0.5m has been set aside for LGR preparatory costs but adds: 'although it is not yet clear whether this will be sufficient, and the financial requirement is likely to evolve as plans progress.' This is a known structural event within the MTFP period that could create unexpected costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty about the council's continued existence and ability to service debt. LGR creates structural uncertainty and the risk that costs could exceed reserves. If LGR requires debt settlement or restructuring, the council's borrowing capacity could be materially affected.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - MTFP and General Fund 2026-27 v2
findings.headline: Council is drawing down £10.3m from reserves in 2026/27 alone to balance the budget, despite revenue appearing to cover base expenditure.
findings.detail: The council's budget requirement is £16.081m but revenue funding (government grants and council tax) only provides £16.081m after Collection Fund deficit adjustment. However, net expenditure is £26.35m, requiring £10.268m contribution from earmarked reserves in 2026/27 to balance. This reserve depletion is expected to continue in future years (£2.353m in 2027/28, £1.594m in 2028/29), depleting the buffers available for managing risks.
findings.matters: Substantial annual reserve drawdowns are not sustainable long-term. They suggest the underlying revenue budget cannot support the scale of capital investment, and if this pattern continues, financial resilience will be eroded. A lender needs to understand why such large drawdowns are required if the budget is 'balanced'.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Harlow KPMG-LG ISA 260 2024-25 v1602
findings.headline: Two related-party organisations with council transactions were not disclosed in the financial statements.
findings.detail: The auditor's Companies House search identified Young Concerns Trust and The Razed Roof Inclusive Theatre Group—entities in which council members had interests and which had conducted transactions with the council—but these were not disclosed. The council's control process reviews only the three largest third-party transactions (Essex County Council, HTS Ltd, Veolia), leaving other related parties undetected. While individually immaterial, this reveals a control deficiency that could allow material related-party activity to escape detection.
findings.matters: Related-party disclosures are a fundamental governance control preventing self-dealing and abuse. A process that misses related parties indicates governance risk and creates the potential for future material related-party activity to go undetected.
findings.figures: 2 related-party entities omitted; transactions individually immaterial
findings.quote: We identified two related parties of members that were not previously disclosed to the Council whereby transactions had occurred in year: Young Concerns Trust and The Razed Roof Inclusive Theatre Group

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Harlow KPMG-LG ISA 260 2024-25 v1602
findings.headline: Cascade audit delay: 2023/24 audit signed 7.5 months late, compressing the 2024/25 audit to failure.
findings.detail: The previous year's audit was not signed until 12 November 2025 (31 March 2024 year-end), preventing the 2024/25 audit from starting until November 2025. This left only three months to complete a full audit before the 27 February 2026 backstop deadline, directly contributing to the current-year disclaimer. The auditor flagged the need to 'ensure the audit can be completed in a more timely manner' in advance of 2025/26.
findings.matters: Serial late completion of audits creates cascading delays that eventually prevent timely verification of accounts, affecting stakeholder confidence in financial reporting and the council's ability to meet regulatory deadlines.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit start: November 2025; backstop: 27 February 2026 (3-month window)
findings.quote: Delays in the 2023/24 audit, which was signed in November 2025, meant we were unable to start the 2024/25 audit until that point and therefore limited work has only been possible on the 2024/25 financial statement audit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Harlow KPMG-LG ISA 260 2024-25 v1602
findings.headline: The council breached three of its own treasury management strategy indicators during 2024/25.
findings.detail: Harlow exceeded its approved risk limits on borrowing maturity structure (policy: max 25% due within 12 months; actual: 32%) and interest rate exposure (policy: £400k-£500k impact per 1% rate movement; actual: £766,213 for both scenarios). The auditor notes there was 'weakness in the application of the indicators in informing decisions'. All three breaches resulted from the Burnt Mills asset acquisition, which required short-term borrowing while awaiting long-term private financing.
findings.matters: These breaches indicate the council's risk management controls did not prevent over-leveraging on an unplanned capital acquisition—a direct signal to lenders about whether the council can stay within its own debt policy limits when making major financial decisions.
findings.figures: Maturity: 25% limit vs 32% actual; Interest rate exposure: £400k-£500k targets vs £766,213 actual
findings.quote: The Council did not comply with three indicators within its Treasury Management Strategy during 2024/25. The first related to the maturity structure of borrowing in which the Council set that a maximum of 25% of its total borrowing should be due within twelve months. The actual proportion at 31st March 2025 was 32%

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Harlow KPMG-LG ISA 260 2024-25 v1602
findings.headline: KPMG will issue a disclaimer of audit opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements due to insufficient time to complete audit work.
findings.detail: The auditor has determined there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves at 31 March 2025 ahead of the 27 February 2026 statutory backstop date. This is pervasive to the council's financial position. Multiple significant audit risks—land and buildings valuation, investment properties valuation, council dwellings valuation, and management override of controls—could not be fully tested before the deadline.
